C01.funFact: Fossilized remains of these distinctive inflated pods have been found dating back to the Pleistocene era in Germany. It is a close relative of the  tomato, and eggplant, but unlike its cousins, almost all parts of this plant (except the ripe fruit) are poisonous due to solanine.

E04.uses: Soups and Stews: The most common culinary use is boiling the leaves into a rich, mucilaginous (slimy) broth. In Egypt, it is minced into the national dish, Molokhia. In Nigeria, it is used to make Ewedu soup, and in the Philippines, it is a staple vegetable known as Saluyot.Thickening Agent: Due to its gelatinous texture (similar to okra), dried and powdered jute mallow leaves are widely used to naturally thicken stews and sauces.Herbal Tea: The leaves are dried and steeped to create a medicinal, antioxidant-rich herbal tea.
E04.funFact: Cleopatra’s Beauty Secret: Legend has it that the famous Egyptian queen, Cleopatra, consumed Molokhia soup daily and used the leaf extracts to maintain her radiant, youthful skin. Fiber Production: The stems of the jute mallow are the primary source of jute fiber (often called the "golden fiber").

Plot1.uses: Traditional medicinal plant. Use to speed  up healing  fractured bones, sprains  joint pain. Widely use for reducing joint inflammation (arthritis)
Plot1.funFact: Veld grape and dragon fruit  look very similar, often causing confusion among gardeners.

L1 A.uses: Landscaping: Used to create lush, tropical privacy screens, borders, or dramatic focal points in gardens.Floral Arrangements: The waxy, hanging bracts are highly prized for professional and home floral arrangements, boasting a vase life of up to 14 days.Wildlife Attraction: The nectar inside the flowers serves as a vital food source for sunbirds.Feng Shui: In tropical design and landscaping, it is sometimes utilized to promote energetic harmony and professional growth
L1 A.funFact: It's a Banana Cousin: It belongs to the Heliconiaceae family and features large, paddle-shaped leaves closely related to bananas and birds-of-paradise.

L1 B.uses: Ornamental: A highly popular outdoor hedge or patio container plant in tropical and subtropical regions, and a coveted novelty houseplant in colder climates.
L1 B.funFact: Thomas Edison historically experimented with this plant alongside hundreds of others while trying to source a domestic alternative for natural rubber.

L1 C.uses: Wound Healing: Often called the "soldier's herb," the leaves are applied topically to minor wounds, insect bites, and ulcers to stop bleeding and ward off infections
L1 C.funFact: According to legend, the plant gets its name from a wounded 19th-century Spanish soldier named Matico. After learning from local Indigenous tribes in Peru that applying the plant's leaves to his battle wounds stopped the bleeding, the herb quickly gained the nickname soldier's herb

L1 D.uses: Culinary: The fruit rind and soft flesh are edible. Sweet varieties are eaten fresh (sometimes dipped in chili salt), while sour varieties are stewed, candied, or used as souring agents in dishes like Filipino sinigang or ginataang santol and Thai curries.
L1 D.funFact: The Toxic Seed Hazard: While the fluffy white pulp is delicious, the large seeds are toxic and must not be swallowed. Swallowing them whole has caused severe intestinal obstruction, occasionally requiring abdominal surgery.

L1 E.uses: Medicinal Applications: The leaves are widely used in poultices and decoctions to treat joint pain, rheumatism, and sprains. In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and Ayurveda, extracts are used to address colds, headaches, skin conditions, and respiratory issues.
L1 E.funFact: The name "chaste tree" stems from the ancient Greek and medieval belief that potions made from the plant acted as an anaphrodisiac. Historically, monks were said to chew the leaves or sleep on beds of the plant to help maintain their vows of celibacy, leading to its alternative nickname, "Monk's pepper"

L1 F.uses: Fresh Consumption: Eaten raw as a thirst-quenching snack, often sprinkled with salt or chili, or sliced into tropical fruit salads
L1 F.funFact: Super Hydrating: The fruit consists of up to 91% water, making it an excellent natural hydrator during hot weather

L1 G.uses: Cosmetics & Body Art: The leaves are dried, milled, and mixed with water to create a paste (mehndi) used for temporary skin tattoos and permanent hair dyeing
L1 G.funFact: Ancient Egyptians used henna paste to stain the hair and fingernails of mummies before burial. The pigment was believed to offer protection and symbolize purification for the afterlife.

L1 H.uses: Natural Dye: The leaves and stems contain a compound called indican, which has been used for centuries to produce the famous natural blue dye known as "Assam Indigo".Traditional Medicine: The rhizomes, roots, and leaves are staples in traditional Chinese medicine (known as Nan Ban Lan Gen or Qingdai). They are used to make herbal decoctions and poultices for their anti-inflammatory, detoxifying, and antiviral properties.
L1 H.funFact: Historically, indigenous cultures combined the blue dye extracted from its twigs with turmeric to create green dyes, or with safflower to create rich purple hues.

L1 I.uses: Culinary: The juicy seeds (arils) are eaten fresh, used to top salads/desserts, or pressed for juice. The juice is also boiled down into grenadine syrup. Highly valued for its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial properties. The arils are an excellent source of vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, and dietary fiber.
L1 I.funFact: The French word for pomegranate is "pomme-grenade," which literally translates to "seeded apple". This fruit inspired the name and design of the hand grenade!

L1 J.uses: Culinary: The translucent, sweet-tart aril is primarily consumed fresh, but it is also used in fruit salads, jams, jellies, and desserts.Industrial & Cooking: The seeds are rich in fats and oils used in soap manufacturing, candle making, and cooking oil. The roasted seeds are also eaten as a snack in some cultures
L1 J.funFact: The Origin of the Name: The word rambutan comes from the Malay-Indonesian word rambut, which translates to "hair". This perfectly describes the fruit's unique, hairy-looking exterior.

L1 K.uses: Culinary: Often called the "Queen of the Lemon Herbs," it is used to flavor teas, baked goods, sauces, and dressings. It is a popular, acid-free substitute for lemon fruit in milk-based desserts like cheesecake or ice cream, as it won't curdle the milk.Health & Wellness: The leaves are rich in citral (the compound giving it the lemon scent), offering natural antiseptic, antifungal, and antibacterial properties.
L1 K.funFact: More lemony than lemon: It contains up to 98% citral, making its natural citrus fragrance and flavor significantly more potent than actual lemons.

L1 L.uses: Fruit consumption: Eaten fresh, blended into milkshakes, or used in desserts like mousses. It is rich in calories, dietary fiber, and vitamins A and B.Latex harvesting: The bark and all parts of the tree exude a milky, gummy sap called chicle. This was the original, primary base for commercial chewing gum and was historically chewed by the Aztecs
L1 L.funFact: Chiku fruits are notorious for their sticky latex content when unripe, which creates an astringent, gummy texture. As the fruit ripens, the latex dissipates, leaving a flavor that has been described as a delicious combination of pear, brown sugar, and cinnamon.

L1 M.uses: Medicinal & Folk Remedies: In traditional medicine throughout Southeast Asia, fresh leaves are crushed to ease inflammation, dermatitis, and insect or snake bites. Decoctions and poultices are also applied to minor skin irritations and cold sores.
L1 M.funFact: The plant’s Latin specific epithet, lupulina, means "wolf." It was given this name because its dense, overlapping flower bracts resemble the unrelated European hop vine (Humulus lupulus).

L1 N.uses: Ornamental Landscaping: Frequently planted as a low, formal hedge or small privacy screen in tropical and subtropical gardens.Bonsai Cultivation: Its small leaves, woody branches, and natural tolerance for heavy trimming make it a favorite choice for shaping into traditional bonsai.
L1 N.funFact: Not a True Holly: Its leaves look like holly with their spiny-toothed margins, which is where it gets its common name, but it belongs to an entirely different plant family.Edible Berries: The flowers (which range from white to pink) develop into edible berries, which can be eaten raw or cooked into jellies and tarts

L 1 O.uses: Noni Juice: The ripened, fermented fruit is pressed into juice, heavily marketed globally as a nutrient-dense dietary supplement and antioxidant booster.Traditional Medicine: For over 2,000 years across Polynesia and Southeast Asia, different parts of the plant were used to treat gastrointestinal distress, infections, pain, and skin inflammation.Natural Dyes: The bark contains a red pigment, and roots yield a bright yellow pigment historically used to dye fabrics and paper.
L 1 O.funFact: Strong Odor: As the fruit ripens, it emits a foul, pungent smell resembling strong, stinky cheese or vomit, giving it the nickname "cheese fruit" or "vomit fruit".Survival Food: Because the tree thrives in harsh coastal sands, volcanic terrain, and drought conditions, it is historically known as "starvation fruit" used by islanders during periods of famine

L1 P.uses: Culinary: The fruit is high in starch and eaten fresh (often with a dash of salt, pepper, or lemon juice). It is incredibly popular for blending into rich, custardy milkshakes, smoothies, and ice creams, or for baking into pies and cupcakes.
L1 P.funFact: During World War II, British pilots and crewmen training in the Bahamas developed a massive fondness for the fruit and bought out all the supply they could find in local markets.

L8 A.uses: Sericulture (Silk Production): White mulberry leaves serve as the primary, indispensable food source for silkworms.Culinary Arts: The sweet, tart fruits are eaten fresh or processed into jams, juices, wines, pies, and tarts.Traditional Medicine: Practitioners of Traditional Chinese Medicine use the root bark, leaves, and fruit to address coughs, fever, and blood sugar regulation.
L8 A.funFact: Not a True Berry: Botanically speaking, a mulberry is not a berry at all but a "multiple fruit" formed from a cluster of independent flowers.Super-Sonic Pollen: The flowers of the white mulberry tree can fire pollen at over half the speed of sound, making it one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.

L8 B.uses: Medicinal Infusions: In the Philippines, the leaves are widely boiled to create a medicinal tea used to treat coughs, diarrhea, colic, and dysentery
L8 B.funFact: Namesake Origins: It gets its name from the Fujian Province in southeastern China (often spelled Fukien in the past), where it has been grown for centuries and is mentioned in literature dating back to the Tang Dynasty.

L8 C.uses: Edible Greens: Highly nutritious and packed with protein and vitamins. The tender leaves are frequently boiled, stir-fried, or used as a nutrient-dense spinach substitute in soups, quiches, and omelettes. The flowers can be eaten raw in salads.
L8 C.funFact: Explosive Seed Pods: The plant produces seed pods that, when ripe and dry, split in half explosively to fling their seeds out into the surrounding area.It’s Not Actually Chinese: Despite its common name, the Chinese Violet is native to sub-Saharan Africa and India

L8 D.uses: Folk Medicine: Traditionally crushed, boiled, or dried to create herbal teas and poultices. It is empirically used to lower blood pressure, reduce cholesterol, manage diabetes, and heal wounds
L8 D.funFact: It’s Not Actually an Onion: Despite resembling shallots with its red skin and white rings, the Dayak onion belongs to the iris family (the same family as saffron) rather than the allium family.Evening Bloomers: The plant produces small, delicate five-petaled white or yellow flowers that bloom in the late afternoon and stay open for only a few hours.

L8 E.uses: Fresh Consumption: Eaten fresh out of hand when absolutely ripe (deep red or near-black) to avoid its bitter, resinous under-ripe tang.
L8 E.funFact: Folk Remedies: Teas made from the leaves are used as a folk treatment for stomachaches, colic, bronchitis, and heartburn.Blood Pressure: Traditional extracts have been studied for their natural antihypertensive properties.

L8 F.uses: The tree is primarily valued for its bright red-orange seeds, which provide a versatile natural pigment called annatto.Natural Food Coloring: It is one of the world's most common natural dyes, used to give cheese (like Cheddar), butter, margarine, ice cream, and rice their yellow or orange hues.
L8 F.funFact: The Name Origin: The "lipstick tree" nickname comes from indigenous people in Central and South America using the seed pulp as a natural cosmetic and body paint for ceremonies.Ancient Sunscreen: The Mayans and Aztecs used the pigment not just for color, but as a natural sunscreen and insect repellent.

L8 G.uses: Used in drinks, marinades, and desserts
L8 G.funFact: Prevented scurvy in sailors; highly acidic fruit.

L8 H.uses: Traditional Medicine: In Southeast Asia (especially Malaysia and Singapore), the raw or boiled leaves are used in folk medicine to treat cancer, rheumatism, gastric pain, and ulcers.Edible Fruits & Leaves: The fleshy, top-shaped yellow fruits are edible (though quite sour) and can be used in chili pastes or cocktails. The leaves can also be eaten raw in small quantities or used to make tea
L8 H.funFact: A Cactus with Leaves: Unlike nearly all other cacti, the Rose Cactus does not drop its leaves; it retains large, glossy green leaves year-round.Ancient Ancestry: Because it retains true leaves, it is considered a "primitive" or non-succulent cactus. It is basically an evolutionary stepping stone between normal leafy shrubs and desert cacti!

L8 I.uses: Herbal Tea: The leaves are traditionally harvested, dried, and brewed into an herbal beverage commonly known as Java Tea.Kidney & Urinary Health: Valued in Southeast Asian traditional medicine for its diuretic properties. It is widely used to promote kidney function, help flush out toxins, and support urinary tract health
L8 I.funFact: Pollinator Magnet: The unique, protruding stamens of the Cat's Whiskers plant are perfectly structured for "buzz pollination," drawing in numerous insects and solitary native bees (such as the blue-banded bee)

L8 J.uses: 1 Turmeric,  2 Black Turmeric,  3 Shell Ginger,   4 Shampoo Ginger,   5 Mango Ginger,   6 Torch Ginger,   7 Blue Ginger,  8 Butterfly Ginger Lily,  9 Crepe Ginger,  10 Red Button Ginger
L8 J.funFact: 1 Turmeric: Standard culinary spice used for vibrant yellow coloring in curries, anti-inflammatory supplements, and natural textiles dyes.  2 Black Turmeric: Rare medicinal root applied as a topical paste for sprains, snakebites, and cosmetic face masks.  3 Shell Ginger: Ornamental plant utilized for wrapping foods, brewing traditional herbal teas, and antioxidant skin care.  4 Shampoo Ginger: Sap from the flower cones serves as a natural, fragrant hair cleanser and scalp moisturizer.  5 Mango Ginger: Distinct raw-mango flavored rhizome ideal for fresh pickles, chutneys, and soothing digestive issues.   6 Torch Ginger: Edible pink flower buds highly prized as an aromatic ingredient in Southeast Asian salads, laksa, and curries.  7 Blue Ginger: Native Galangal variety primarily used to add a sharp, citrusy-earthy bite to Thai pastes and Indonesian dishes. 8 Butterfly Ginger Lily : Known for their intense, sweet fragrance, the fresh flowers are edible and frequently used as an aromatic garnish in salads, teas, and desserts. 9 Crepe Ginger: Multiple parts of the plant, including the flowers, leaves, shoots, and rhizomes, are safely consumed in traditional Southeast Asian and Indian cooking. 10 Red Button Ginger: Yes, red button ginger is edible, particularly its bright yellow flowers and the surrounding red cone-shaped bracts.
L8 J.botanical: Turmeric: Curcuma longa,  Black Turmeric: Curcuma caesia,  Shell Ginger: Alpinia zerumbet,  Shampoo Ginger: Zingiber zerumbet,  Mango Ginger: Curcuma amada,  Torch Ginger: Etlingera elatior,  Blue Ginger: Alpinia galanga, Butterfly Ginger Lily: Hedychium coronarium, Crepe ginger: Cheilocostus speciosus , Red button ginger:  Costus woodsonii

L8 K.uses: Culinary: The leaves are a staple leafy vegetable in many West and Central African cuisines (most famously in the Nigerian dish Ofe Onugbu). Because of their pungency, they are repeatedly squeezed and washed to remove excess bitterness before being added to stews.Traditional Medicine: The juice and leaf extracts are consumed as tonics or teas to alleviate malaria, control blood sugar in diabetics, and boost digestion.
L8 K.funFact: Domestic Applications: The strong, bitter woody stems are frequently broken down and used as natural "chewing sticks" to maintain dental hygiene and ward off mouth infections.

L8 L.uses: Skin Healing: It is widely known as the "ringworm bush". Crushed fresh leaves or sap contain chrysophanic acid, which naturally fights fungal infections like ringworm, athlete's foot, and eczema when applied topically.
L8 L.funFact: The candle bush gets its name because its unopened bright-yellow flower spikes resemble giant, glowing, waxy candles!

L8 M.uses: Culinary: Tubers are a rich source of complex carbohydrates and are eaten baked, boiled, mashed, or pounded into fufu. Purple varieties (Dioscorea alata) are prized for making desserts and ice cream.Nutritional: They provide high levels of dietary fiber, vitamin C, potassium, and B-complex vitamins.Medicinal: Yam tubers contain a compound called diosgenin. This plant steroid is widely used in the pharmaceutical industry to synthesize steroidal hormones, including those used in birth control pills
L8 M.funFact: Not Sweet Potatoes! In the United States, orange-fleshed sweet potatoes are frequently mislabeled and sold as "yams". True yams are starchy with a bark-like, rough skin, whereas sweet potatoes are much sweeter and have a thin, smooth skin.

L8 N.uses: Insect Repellent: The oil contains natural compounds (like citronellal, geraniol, and limonene) that mask human odors, effectively deterring mosquitoes and other biting bugs [1].Aromatherapy: Used in diffusers to create a calming, refreshing atmosphere and to help relieve mental fatigue.Skincare & Cosmetics: Diluted into soaps, lotions, and massage oils [2]. It has natural antifungal and antibacterial properties that help cleanse the skin.
L8 N.funFact: Not a single plant: People often assume citronella is a specific plant, but it is actually a tall, clumping grass similar to lemongrass

L8 O.uses: Culinary: The mushroom-flavored flowers are a popular, quirky addition to fresh salads. The tough flower spikes can also be used as a seasoning in soups and stews much like a bay leaf.Traditional Medicine: Historically used by indigenous and folk healers as a "cooling tonic". Leaves are frequently steeped into teas or decoctions to help soothe gastrointestinal discomfort, clear respiratory issues, and promote relaxation
L8 O.funFact: It tastes like mushrooms: The tiny, delicate flowers can be eaten raw and have a surprisingly distinct, earthy, mushroom-like flavor.It has a beer connection: The common name "porterweed" comes from the dark, foamy, beer-like infusion that can be made from brewing its leaves.

L8 P.uses: Culinary & Beverages: The soft, white flesh is blended into refreshing smoothies, juices, ice creams, and jams. It has a unique flavor often described as a mix of strawberry, pineapple, and citrus.Traditional Medicine: In many tropical regions, teas made from the leaves and bark are used to treat ailments like inflammation, fevers, and insomnia.v
L8 P.funFact: Electric Leaves: The leaves and roots of the soursop tree are known to contain chemical compounds (annonacins) that are highly toxic to certain pests. Studies have shown they can even disrupt the nervous systems of small insects.

L8 Q.uses: This plant is a powerhouse in traditional medicine and regional cuisines across South and Southeast Asia:Medicinal Tea: The leaves are frequently brewed into a health-promoting tea, particularly in Thailand, to manage conditions like diabetes and rheumatism.
L8 Q.funFact: VapoRub Scent: When its leaves are crushed, they release a powerful, medicinal odor similar to camphor or Vicks VapoRub, which gives the plant its name.Antioxidant Powerhouse: Research suggests that tea made from Pluchea indica leaves can have stronger antioxidant properties than even green tea (Camellia sinensis). Coastal Guardian: This plant thrives in harsh, salty environments like mangroves and salt marshes, playing a vital role in maintaining the ecological balance of coastal areas.Natural Insect Repellent: Because of its pungent chemical glands, the plant is naturally resistant to deer and is often used as a biological insect repellent.

L8 R.uses: Traditionally, various parts of the plant are used in Ayurvedic and other traditional systems of medicine to treat skin complaints, diarrhea, vertigo, fever, and body aches.  The ripe, dark purple or black berries are edible and have a tart, pleasant taste. They are sometimes used in jams and jellies.
L8 R.funFact: The fruit is a favorite snack of the bandicoot, a small marsupial, which gives the plant its common name, Bandicoot Berry.

L8 S.uses: When ripe, they are dark red or purple, crunchy, and refreshing, similar to an apple. Used in soups, stews, porridges, and as a filling for Chinese desserts like mooncakes and mochi.
L8 S.funFact: Jujube fruit , also known as red dates  is a highly nutritious, versatile fruit cultivated for over 4,000 years, primarily in Asia

L8 T.uses: Digestive Aid: Chewing fresh leaves after meals stimulates saliva and digestive juices. It helps reduce bloating and constipation.Oral Hygiene: Naturally antibacterial, the leaf helps combat oral pathogens that cause cavities, gum disease, and bad breath.Respiratory Relief: It has anti-inflammatory and expectorant properties. Applying a warm poultice to the chest or consuming the leaf juice with honey can help relieve coughs and chest congestion.Wound Healing: Applied topically as a crushed paste, it acts as an antiseptic to promote faster healing of small cuts and skin infections.
L8 T.funFact: Green Gold": Because of its widespread daily consumption and numerous health benefits, it is sometimes referred to as the "Green Gold" of India.The Fourth Most Popular Drug: Betel chewing (wrapping the leaf with the areca/betel nut and slaked lime) is considered the fourth most popular psychoactive drug in the world, surpassed only by nicotine, alcohol, and caffeine.

L8 U.uses: Broom Production: Its long, feathery flower panicles are harvested and dried to create durable "light dust" brooms (often called phool jhadu) that are staples in households across South and Southeast Asia.
L8 U.funFact: Disney Famous: This grass is planted extensively at Disneyland, particularly around the Jungle Cruise ride, to create an authentic tropical jungle atmosphere.

L8 V.uses: Traditional Medicine: The plant has a long history in Southeast Asian and Javanese traditional medicine. Leaves, twigs, and sap are often used in poultices to soothe fevers, heal wounds, treat headaches, and address bodily pain.
L8 V.funFact: Thorny All the Way: Unlike many other Leea species, L. angulata is fiercely protected by sharp, triangular prickles that cover not just its trunk and main branches, but its ultimate, tender branches as well.Grape Family Ties: It belongs to the Vitaceae family (the grape family). However, unlike its trailing or climbing grapevine cousins, it grows as a strong, upright, multi-stemmed shrub or tree.Critically Endangered in Singapore: If you are based in Punggol or elsewhere in Singapore, it might be very hard to spot. In local botany records, the plant is listed as Critically Endangered in the wild, with only a few pockets of adult individuals documented (such as around the Lower Seletar Reservoir).

L8 W.uses: The flowers are a specialty ingredient in Thai, Vietnamese, and Filipino cuisine. They are commonly cooked into omelets, stir-fried with oyster sauce, or used in soups.
L8 W.funFact: The flowers emit a very strong, pleasant citrus-like fragrance, particularly during the evening. This oil is extracted to create perfumes and in floral, aromatic gardens. That is why its Chinese name is 夜来香

L8 X.uses: Culinary & Snacks: Eaten roasted or salted, and blended into pastes as the creamy base for Indian curries (like Korma)
L8 X.funFact: They Are Not True Nuts: Botanically, the cashew is actually a drupe (a seed that grows on the outside of a false fruit), rather than a traditional nut.A Poison Ivy Relative: The cashew tree is in the Anacardiaceae family, meaning it shares a botanical lineage with pistachios, mangoes, and toxic plants like poison ivy and poison oak

L8 Y.uses: Fresh Eating: The fruit is typically eaten fresh; it is scooped out and best served chilled.
L8 Y.funFact: The "Star" Pattern: When the fruit is sliced in half horizontally, the core and seeds create a beautiful, distinct star-like pattern.

L8 Z.uses: Fresh Eating: Sliced raw and eaten fresh, often used as a garnish in salads, fruit platters, and cocktails.
L8 Z.funFact: Dietary Precaution: People with kidney problems or chronic kidney disease should avoid star fruit National Kidney Foundation. The fruit contains a neurotoxin (carambotoxin) and high levels of oxalates that healthy kidneys easily filter out, but can be dangerous or cause severe hiccups, vomiting, and confusion in individuals with kidney dysfunction.

L8 ZA.uses: Culinary: Used to flavor baked goods, salads, and marinades, and to preserve jams. The fresh juice is also a staple for making lemonade and flavoring teas
L8 ZA.funFact: Glowing Spark: When the oils from a lemon peel are squeezed near an open flame, the compounds (specifically limonene) ignite to create a tiny spark, essentially functioning as a natural firework.

L8 ZC.uses: Culinary Snack (Emping): The mature seeds are ground into flour and deep-fried to create emping, a popular, slightly bitter Indonesian cracker.
L8 ZC.funFact: An Imposter "Fruit": Melinjo does not produce true fruits or flowers. It is a gymnosperm (related to pine trees), meaning its "fruits" are actually colorful, fleshy seed cones.

L8 ZD.uses: Culinary: Highly sour, it is used as a natural souring agent (like tamarind) in Asian curries, fish stews, and sambals. In Southeast Asia and the Philippines, the raw fruit is often dipped in rock salt or made into sweet jams and pickles.Traditional Medicine: The leaves, fruit, and flowers are used in folk medicine to treat coughs, high blood pressure, and skin conditions (like itchy rashes or mumps).
L8 ZD.funFact: Grows from the trunk: Unlike most fruits that hang from branches, belimbing fruits grow in heavy, clustered groups directly on the tree trunk and main branches.High productivity: A single tree can produce an astonishing 45 to 50 kg of fruit in a year.

L8 ZE.uses: Beverage production: Roasted and ground seeds are brewed into global beverage variants.Caffeine extraction: Isolates are utilized in pharmaceuticals, energy drinks, and supplements.
L8 ZE.funFact: Fruit origins: Coffee beans are actually seeds found inside bright red fruits called "coffee cherries".Goat discovery: Legend says 9th-century Ethiopian herders discovered coffee after seeing goats "dance" from eating the berries.

L14 A.uses: Leaves: Known as one of the most nutrient-dense foods on earth. They are cooked like spinach or dried and ground into a powder for use in smoothies and teas.
L14 A.funFact: Nutritional Super-Punch: Ounce for ounce, moringa leaves are said to provide 7 times more vitamin C than oranges, 10 times more vitamin A than carrots, and 17 times more calcium than milk.

L14 B.uses: Culinary Preserves: The mature fruits are highly acidic and astringent when eaten fresh, so they are rarely consumed raw. They are popularly cooked with generous amounts of sugar to make jams, syrups, jellies, and tarts
L14 B.funFact: Not a True Plum: Despite its name, the Batoko plum is actually a berry. It belongs to the willow family (Salicaceae), rather than being related to the traditional stone-fruit plums (genus Prunus )

L14 C.uses: Food & Confectionery: The seeds (cacao beans) are fermented, dried, and roasted to create cocoa mass, which is the foundation of all chocolate products
L14 C.funFact: Tiny Pollinators: The tree's pale, intricate flowers are not pollinated by bees. Instead, they rely exclusively on tiny biting midges (Forcipomyia flies).Fruit Makeup: Inside each football-shaped pod, the seeds are surrounded by a sweet, sticky white pulp that is delicious to eat raw.

L14 D.uses: Fresh Eating: The fruit is typically eaten fresh; it is scooped out and best served chilled.
L14 D.funFact: The "Star" Pattern: When the fruit is sliced in half horizontally, the core and seeds create a beautiful, distinct star-like pattern.

L14 E.uses: Fresh Consumption: The snow-white, segmented interior flesh (aril) is juicy and tastes like a blend of peach, citrus, and vanilla.Desserts & Beverages: Used globally to make jams, sorbets, ice creams, and jellies.Traditional Medicine: The thick, deep-purple rind (pericarp) is dried and used in folk and Ayurvedic medicine to treat diarrhea, dysentery, skin infections, and wounds.Nutritional Supplements:
L14 E.funFact: Royal Nickname: The fruit earned its moniker, the "Queen of Fruits," largely due to a legendary (though unverified) tale that Queen Victoria offered a reward to anyone who could bring her a fresh mangosteen.The "King and Queen": In Southeast Asia, it is the perfect pairing for the durian, which is dubbed the "King of Fruits". Eating mangosteen is traditionally said to have a cooling effect that neutralizes the "heaty" properties of durian.
